J.P. Morgan - European Credit Research
Ocado
Ocado Smart Carry
By Neill Keaney AC
Click here for the full document and disclaimers

We initiate on the Ocado credit and its outstanding SUNs with an Overweight
recommendation. Credit strength is underpinned by a shift from cash-burning online grocery
pureplay to asset-backed retail technology and logistics platform. Technology Solutions is
now the main EBITDA engine, with live-module economics, recurring capacity fees and a
growing international footprint supporting our view that the existing module portfolio more than
covers the debt stack even before assigning value to future contract wins, SBA trials or ORL.
Whilst strong ytd returns mean that the opportunity is now largely carry-based, it is a
compelling one: The 11% coupon means a running yield of almost 10.5% with nearly one
year of call protection remaining.

recommendation. We will discuss the investment case from both sides of the balance sheet
centred around our aligned thesis that valuation is unchallenged given the present value of

From online grocery pureplay to one-stop retail technology business: Founded in 2000 as
a pure-play online supermarket in the UK, Ocado is now more accurately described as a
technology solutions partner for an international network of grocery retailers. Ocado now
generates profit through two distinct but complimentary businesses: Technology Solutions,
which offers vertically integrated software and physical retail solutions, predominantly via the
Ocado Smart Platform (OSP) and Ocado Logistics, which provides fulfilment services to
Ocado’s UK clients, including Ocado Retail Limited (ORL). The heritage online supermarket is
outside the Restricted Group and bondholders have no claim on Ocado’s 50% stake, but it
remains a key proof point for the OSP model and a potential source of shareholder-loan
recovery.
Valuation unchallenged: Existing active modules imply almost £2.8bn of EV at £24m per
module, driving an estimated 24% LTV after £765m of cash against the £1.8bn debt stack.
Additional contract signings - more likely now we expect given exclusivity has rolled off in key
markets such as the US - and the potential for a contract win or even an announcement of a trial
of Ocado’s store-based automation (SBA) system, both serve as free options, further supporting
our estimate of asset coverage.
Cash and balance sheet rehabilitation: The prospect of balance sheet rehabilitation is
credible in our view as cost savings, stronger Solutions EBITDA and lower capex offset the
historic bear case around structural cash burn. Management’s guidance for positive cash flow in
4Q26 and FY27 depends most on capex discipline, with our model assuming no uncommitted
CFC expansion. Liquidity is ample, including £765m of cash and a £300m undrawn RCF,
allowing repayment of the £350m January 2027 convert and potentially further debt reduction
through the 10% 103 soft call on the 2030 notes. We expect net leverage, on a ratio basis, to
decline to 3.9x at FY26 from 4.9x at 1H26 and to 2.3x by FY28.
A renewed focus on profitability and cash flow support management guidance : Ocado
has long framed high cash burn as a positive, being that it signifies strong demand for its capex-
intensive Solutions business. The corollary, of course, is a consistent need for fresh capital.
However, as new orders have dried up and existing clients (Kroger, Sobey’s) have closed
existing CFCs or cancelled planned openings, cash flow has been inadvertently supported by
significantly lower CFC capex. We expect stronger underlying EBITDA, driven by recurring fee
income and cost savings at Tech Solutions and lower Group-level capex to deliver a very
modest positive (+£2.6m) cash flow in FY27, in line with management guidance.
In this note we expand on the above the points, present summary models including at the
consolidated Group-level but also for Tech Solutions, Ocado Logistics and ORL as well as
offering deep dives into all three divisions. We also outline our expectations for cash flow,
including the crucial variable of capex, over the next three years. Risks to our recommendation
include uneven international adoption, the cash drag from major new CFC wins, a porous
covenant package, and new debt incurrence
